title: Travelers' Third-Quarter Profit Edges Up to $1.92 Billion as Catastrophe Losses Rise to $538 Million and Investment Income Hits a Record
summary: Travelers reported net income of $1.917 billion and a combined ratio of 86.8% for the quarter, with net written premiums of $11.48 billion; catastrophe losses rose from the prior year but nine-month catastrophe losses are about half of last year's.
description:
Travelers Companies, one of the largest property and casualty insurers in the United States, reported third-quarter 2026 results on October 16 that show strong profit despite a heavier burden of storm losses than a year earlier. Net income was $1.917 billion, compared with $1.888 billion in the third quarter of 2025. Core income, which strips out investment gains and losses, was $1.947 billion against $1.867 billion. The figures below come from Reinsurance News and Insurance Journal, which both reported the results. We have not reviewed Travelers' own release. Where the two reports differ, we say so. Amounts are in US dollars.

The key measure for an insurer is the combined ratio: claims plus expenses divided by premiums earned. Below 100% means an underwriting profit. Travelers' combined ratio was 86.8%, an improvement of 0.5 points on the same quarter a year earlier, according to Reinsurance News. That report explains the movement: favourable development of prior-year reserves, meaning that claims from earlier years turned out cheaper than expected, improved the ratio by 1.9 points; higher catastrophe losses worsened it by 1.2 points; and a higher underlying combined ratio added 0.2 points. The underlying combined ratio, which excludes catastrophes and reserve development, was 84.1%. Insurance Journal's text gives the combined ratio as 'an efficient 8%', which looks like a typographical error; the segment ratios in the same article point to a figure in the high 80s, consistent with 86.8%. Favourable prior-year reserve development was $234 million before tax and came from three segments.

Catastrophe losses were $538 million, mainly from severe wind and hail storms in multiple states. The comparison figure for the third quarter of 2025 differs between the two reports: Reinsurance News says $302 million and Insurance Journal says $402 million. We could not reconcile this, and readers who need the number should check Travelers' release. Either way, losses were higher than a year earlier. Net written premiums, the premiums the company wrote after reinsurance, were $11.48 billion, a slight increase. Excluding Travelers' divested Canadian operations, which contributed $240 million to the prior-year quarter according to Reinsurance News, premiums rose 2%.

The segment detail comes from Insurance Journal. Business Insurance, which serves companies, wrote $5.868 billion of net written premiums, up 4% when adjusted for the Canadian sale. New business was a third-quarter record of $699 million, retention was 86%, and the combined ratio was 88.9%. Growth came from every line except property. Bond and Specialty Insurance wrote $1.209 billion, up 12%, the fastest growth of the three segments; surety premiums rose 21%, and in management liability, renewal premium rose 3.8%, new business rose 18% and retention was 89%. Personal Insurance, which covers auto and homeowners policies, wrote $4.403 billion, down 7%, or down 3% excluding $167 million that came from the Canadian business in the year-earlier quarter. Retention in auto and homeowners was stable, and the segment combined ratio improved to 83.5% despite catastrophe losses from wind and hail. The reports do not give the segment's average rate changes, so we cannot say how pricing moved.

Investment income was also a highlight. Insurance Journal reports record net investment income of $1.098 billion before tax, up 6%. For the first nine months, Reinsurance News gives net investment income of $3.176 billion before tax, up 9%. Insurers invest premiums until claims are paid, so higher bond yields over recent years have lifted this income. Net realised investment losses were $34 million before tax in the quarter, against a gain of $27 million a year earlier.

The nine-month figures show why the year looks strong. Net income was $5.836 billion, up $2.044 billion, and core income was $5.803 billion, up $1.989 billion, which Reinsurance News attributes mainly to lower catastrophe losses. The combined ratio for the period was 86.3%, an improvement of 6.9 points, of which 5.4 points came from lower catastrophe losses. The underlying combined ratio was 84.5%. Natural catastrophe losses were $1.817 billion, down from $3.595 billion. Favourable prior-year reserve development reached $1.225 billion, up from $715 million. In other words, much of the improvement over last year reflects the absence of the very large catastrophe losses that hit the first half of 2025, as the sources frame it.

What did management say? Chairman and chief executive Alan Schnitzer said the company was 'pleased to report excellent third quarter results', and Insurance Journal quotes him describing 'very strong underwriting performance across all three segments' and 'a record result from our investment portfolio'. He said the company is 'well positioned to finish the year strong' with 'real confidence heading into 2027 and beyond'. These are management's statements, not independent assessments. The reports do not give earnings per share or the share price reaction, so we do not comment on how investors received the numbers.

What does it mean for customers? Insurers with combined ratios in the mid-80s are making a healthy underwriting profit, which gives them room to compete on price and to keep writing business in storm-exposed states. The reports do not say that premiums will fall, and Travelers' results by themselves do not predict what happens to an individual household's premium, which depends on the state, the insurer's rates, the home's age and location, and claims experience. The result does show that the hail and wind season was costly: $538 million in one quarter is a large figure even for a company this size. Readers who want more should check Travelers' earnings release and its filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. This article is a news summary and not investment or insurance advice.
source_name: Reinsurance News and Insurance Journal (reporting Travelers' Q3 2026 results, October 16, 2026)
image_alt: Insurance documents and calculator representing quarterly results (illustrative)
key_points: Travelers reported third-quarter 2026 net income of $1.917 billion, up from $1.888 billion, and core income of $1.947 billion, up from $1.867 billion.

The combined ratio was 86.8%, 0.5 points better than a year earlier; favourable prior-year reserve development of $234 million helped by 1.9 points, while higher catastrophe losses cost 1.2 points. The underlying combined ratio was 84.1%.
Catastrophe losses were $538 million, mainly from severe wind and hail storms in several states; net written premiums were $11.48 billion, up about 2% excluding the divested Canadian business.
Net investment income reached a record $1.098 billion before tax, up 6%, according to Insurance Journal.
For nine months, net income was $5.836 billion, the combined ratio 86.3% and natural catastrophe losses $1.817 billion against $3.595 billion a year earlier.
why_it_matters: Travelers is the largest US commercial insurer by many measures, so its results are a read on how well American insurers are covering their claims costs. This quarter shows strong underwriting profit even in a stormy summer, which helps explain why insurers are not cutting prices more aggressively.

title: UnitedHealth Raises 2026 Profit Outlook to at Least $20.50 a Share as Its Medical Care Ratio Improves to 88.4% and Membership Shrinks
summary: UnitedHealth's adjusted earnings were $4.69 a share against $2.92 a year earlier, helped by $610 million of favourable reserve development; revenue was $112.7 billion, slightly lower than last year, and UnitedHealthcare served 48.3 million people against 50.1 million.
description:
UnitedHealth Group, the largest health insurer in the United States, reported third-quarter 2026 results on October 13 that show a sharp recovery in profit and a smaller business. Adjusted diluted earnings were $4.69 per share, compared with $2.92 a year earlier, and the company raised its outlook for the full year. This article is based on UnitedHealth's earnings release, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, and on a news report of the results from Coin Alert News, a site that mainly covers cryptocurrency, so we use the latter only for market details that the release does not contain and label them. All amounts are in US dollars.

Start with the headline figures from the release. Revenue was $112.7 billion, slightly lower than the $113.2 billion of the third quarter of 2025. Earnings from operations were $6.6 billion, up from $4.3 billion, and net earnings were $4.3 billion, up from $2.5 billion, which is a net margin of 3.6% against 2.1%. Diluted earnings per share were $4.56 on a GAAP basis, against $2.59, and $4.69 adjusted, against $2.92. The news report says the adjusted figure beat a consensus of $4.14 and that revenue was above an estimate of $111.40 billion. Those consensus numbers are from the news site and we have not verified them.

The medical care ratio, the share of premiums paid out in medical costs, improved to 88.4% from 89.9%. That includes $610 million of favourable development of prior-period reserves related to 2026 dates of service, meaning the company's earlier estimates of this year's claims proved too high. Without that benefit the ratio would have been higher; the release does not give an adjusted figure, and we do not calculate one. The operating cost ratio fell to 12.8% from 13.5%. Chief financial officer Wayne DeVeydt said, according to the news report, that medical costs 'remain elevated relative to historical norms', so the improvement does not mean costs have gone back to where they were before the pressures of recent years. Chief executive Stephen Hemsley said the results 'reflect the discipline and execution our teams are bringing to every part of our business'.

The outlook was raised. The release says full-year 2026 adjusted diluted earnings per share are now expected to be at least $20.50, and GAAP diluted earnings per share at least $19.50, with projected net earnings attributable to shareholders of more than $17.65 billion on a GAAP basis and more than $18.59 billion adjusted. Coin Alert News reports that the previous adjusted guidance was $19.50 to $20.00 and that the new figure is above an analyst consensus of $19.86. The release does not provide an outlook for full-year revenue or the medical care ratio.

The business is shrinking in membership. UnitedHealthcare, the insurance arm, had revenue of $86.3 billion, against $87.1 billion, and earnings of $2.8 billion, against $1.8 billion, an operating margin of 3.3% against 2.1%. It served 48.3 million people, down from 50.1 million a year earlier. By line, the release lists 29.8 million in commercial plans, 7.6 million in Medicare Advantage, 6.7 million in Medicaid and 4.2 million in Medicare Supplement. The news report says membership fell across employer, Medicaid and Medicare Advantage lines and that 935,000 members have left Medicare Advantage since the end of 2025. We have not verified that last figure against the release. The release does not explain the declines, but insurers commonly reduce membership by withdrawing from unprofitable markets or raising prices, and we have no evidence in these sources of the reasons in this case.

Optum, the health services arm, had revenue of $66.9 billion, against $69.2 billion, and earnings of $3.7 billion, against $2.5 billion, a margin of 5.6% against 3.6%. Optum Health, which provides care, had revenue of $22.9 billion, down 10%, but earnings of $735 million, compared with $41 million a year earlier. Optum Insight earned $1.3 billion on revenue of $5.5 billion, up 3%. Optum Rx, the pharmacy benefit manager, had revenue of $39.9 billion, against $39.7 billion, and earnings of $1.7 billion; adjusted scripts fell to 393 million from 414 million.

The cash flow and balance sheet data are in the release. Operating cash flow was $5.1 billion, or 1.2 times net income, and $25.1 billion for nine months. The debt-to-capital ratio was 41.7%, up from 41.2% in the second quarter, with a target of about 40% by year-end. Year-to-date share repurchases were $5.0 billion and dividends paid $6.2 billion. The news report adds that the shares first rose and then reversed during the day, trading at $376.61 late in the afternoon, down 0.51%, but we treat this as a snapshot and not a verdict.

What should readers take from it? For investors, the results show that UnitedHealth's profitability has recovered through tighter pricing, cost control and reserve releases, at the expense of a smaller membership base. For employers and individuals, the shrinkage in membership suggests that the company is choosing which business to keep, and people who see their plan changed or withdrawn at renewal should compare alternatives. For policymakers, the continued fall in Medicare Advantage membership at the largest insurer is relevant to the debate about that program's financing. The sources do not tell us what is happening at other insurers. This article is a news summary and is not investment or insurance advice.
source_name: UnitedHealth Group (Form 8-K earnings release, October 13, 2026) and Coin Alert News
image_alt: Hospital corridor representing health insurance and care costs (illustrative)
key_points: UnitedHealth reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $112.7 billion (against $113.2 billion), net earnings of $4.3 billion and adjusted diluted earnings of $4.69 a share (against $2.92).
The medical care ratio improved to 88.4% from 89.9%, including $610 million of favourable prior-period reserve development; the operating cost ratio fell to 12.8% from 13.5%.
Full-year 2026 adjusted earnings guidance was raised to at least $20.50 a share (previously $19.50 to $20.00, according to Coin Alert News), and GAAP earnings to at least $19.50.

UnitedHealthcare served 48.3 million people, down from 50.1 million a year earlier, with Medicare Advantage at 7.6 million; one report says 935,000 members have left Medicare Advantage since the end of 2025.
Optum revenue was $66.9 billion (against $69.2 billion) with earnings of $3.7 billion; Optum Health earned $735 million against $41 million a year earlier.
why_it_matters: UnitedHealth is the largest US health insurer, so its medical cost trends are a gauge for the whole health system. Better margins at the cost of fewer members show how insurers are repricing and shrinking unprofitable business, which affects employers and Medicare Advantage enrollees.

title: ASIC's 2026-27 Priorities Letter to General Insurers Targets 'Disaster Chasers', Unclear Motor Renewal Notices and Cash Settlements After Cyclone Jasper
summary: In a letter dated September 30, 2026, ASIC Commissioner Alan Kirkland told insurer boards it will review for-profit claims management firms, found that no sampled motor insurer explained why premiums changed, and said at least 63% of finalised Cyclone Jasper home claims included a cash settlement.
description:
Australia's corporate and financial services regulator has set out what it will look at in the general insurance industry over the year to mid-2027, and it names practices that affect ordinary policyholders: how motor renewal notices explain price changes, how insurers settle storm claims with cash, and a new group of firms that sell help with claims. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) sent a supervisory letter on its 2026-27 general insurance sector priorities, dated September 30, 2026, from Commissioner Alan Kirkland to insurer boards and executives. This article draws on the letter itself. It falls under ASIC's wider priority of improving outcomes for consumers and small business. The letter sets no firm deadlines beyond the start of one review and a consultation held in July 2026.

The first new item concerns what ASIC calls 'disaster chasers'. ASIC says it will review for-profit claims management firms that help consumers with home insurance claims. Its concerns include the firms' sales tactics, their fee and cancellation terms, the role they play in claims and complaints, and their relationships with repairers. The review began in the first quarter of 2026-27, which is July to September 2026, and ASIC will gather information from both insurers and the firms. The letter does not say how many firms there are or how much they charge, so we cannot size the problem. Homeowners who are approached after a disaster should know that their insurer handles claims without charging a fee for doing so, and that they can complain to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority, a point that is general background and not part of the letter.

The second new item is the General Insurance Code of Practice. The Insurance Council of Australia, the industry body, plans to ask ASIC to approve a new code after a public consultation in July 2026. ASIC will assess the draft against its Regulatory Guide 183 and consult stakeholders. A code sets standards of service that insurers promise to follow, and ASIC approval gives it more weight. The letter also says insurers may be included in ASIC reviews of the quality of sustainability reporting, corporate governance and financial reporting.

The letter then returns to two continuing concerns. The first is motor vehicle premium disclosure, which ASIC examined in a report numbered REP 838. According to the letter, no sampled insurer explained the key drivers of the premium or why the premium had changed. Renewal notices often did not make clear that paying the annual premium in one go could save 10% to 20% compared with paying in instalments. Five insurers did not compare changes in the excess or the insured value from one year to the next. ASIC gave individual feedback to insurers and will continue to monitor. It expects clearer quotes and renewals that explain the drivers of the premium, show how the excess, the level of cover and the payment method affect the price, state the cost of paying by instalments compared with annually, and highlight year-on-year changes. For consumers, this is practical: a renewal notice that shows the old and new excess and sum insured side by side makes it far easier to see whether a price rise is for the same cover.

The second continuing concern is cash settlements in home building claims following Cyclone Jasper. ASIC found that at least 63% of finalised home claims included a cash settlement, where the insurer pays an amount of money instead of arranging the repair. The offers were often based on quotes from the insurer's preferred suppliers, which raises doubts about whether the amount covers the real cost of repairs. ASIC also found that consumers needed clearer information about their settlements and review rights, that vulnerable consumers were not always identified or supported, and that insurers held insufficient data on how offers changed after a customer questioned them. ASIC called on all insurers to act and said it would monitor improvements through its supervisory program. The letter does not give the value of the settlements or how many claims were involved in absolute terms, and we do not estimate them.

How will ASIC work with other bodies? The letter says it will coordinate with the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA), the Australian Financial Complaints Authority and the General Insurance Code Governance Committee to avoid duplication. It will also work with other members of the Council of Financial Regulators on emerging cyber risks and on simplifying data collection under the council's Better Regulation Roadmap, and it invites insurers to share practical examples of unnecessary regulatory burden. The letter does not address add-on insurance or the general standards for claims handling in detail.

What should policyholders do? When a motor policy renews, compare the new excess, sum insured and premium with last year's and ask the insurer to explain any large change; check whether paying annually is cheaper than instalments, since the letter says the saving can be 10% to 20%. After a storm, be careful about accepting a cash offer without understanding what it covers, ask for the repair quote on which it is based and ask about the right to a review, and be wary of firms that approach you offering to manage a claim for a fee. What should insurers do? According to ASIC, boards and executives should treat the letter as a statement of expectations, and they should expect follow-up supervision. Readers can find the letter on ASIC's website. This article is a summary of a regulator's letter and is not legal or insurance advice.
source_name: ASIC (supervisory letter to general insurers, September 30, 2026)
image_alt: Storm-damaged roof representing home insurance claims (illustrative)
key_points: ASIC will review for-profit firms that help consumers with home insurance claims, including those it calls 'disaster chasers', looking at sales tactics, fee and cancellation terms, their role in claims and complaints, and their relationships with repairers.

On motor premium disclosure (report REP 838), ASIC found no sampled insurer explained the key drivers of premiums or why they changed, and five did not compare year-on-year changes in excess or insured value.
Renewal notices often did not make clear that paying annually could save 10% to 20% compared with instalments, according to the letter.
After Cyclone Jasper, at least 63% of finalised home claims included a cash settlement, often based on preferred-supplier quotes, which raises doubts about whether offers cover repair costs.
The Insurance Council of Australia plans to seek ASIC approval for a new General Insurance Code of Practice after public consultation in July 2026; ASIC will assess it under RG 183.
why_it_matters: Australians who have had a storm, flood or cyclone claim know how much depends on how insurers settle and explain their decisions. A regulator telling boards exactly what it expects on pricing disclosure and cash settlements sets out the standard that insurers will be judged on.

title: HDFC Life's Half-Year Profit Rises 12.7% to ₹1,119 Crore and Value of New Business Grows 12% as Quarterly Profit Falls From the First Quarter
summary: For the six months to September 30, 2026, India's HDFC Life reported profit after tax of ₹1,119 crore, value of new business of ₹2,037 crore (up 12.1%) at a 24.7% margin, and assets under management of about ₹4.1 lakh crore; second-quarter profit was ₹508 crore, 16.9% lower than the first quarter.
description:
HDFC Life Insurance Company, one of India's biggest private-sector life insurers, announced results for the second quarter and first half of the 2026-27 financial year (FY27) on October 15, 2026. The headline is a half-year profit after tax of ₹1,119 crore, up 12.7% from ₹994 crore, and a value of new business of ₹2,037 crore, up 12.1%. This article draws on a Kotak Neo report on the half-year results, updated on October 16, and a Univest summary of the quarterly figures. We have not reviewed HDFC Life's own press release or investor presentation, and the reports do not include management quotes, the solvency ratio, the persistency ratio or any dividend, so we do not comment on those. A crore is ten million rupees.

Start with profit. Second-quarter profit after tax was ₹508 crore, compared with ₹448.29 crore in the same quarter a year earlier, an increase of 13.3%. Revenue was ₹21,727 crore against ₹18,871 crore, up 15.1%. Against the first quarter of FY27, profit fell 16.9% from ₹611.19 crore. That sequential fall is consistent with the half-year total: ₹611.19 crore plus ₹508 crore comes to about ₹1,119 crore. The reports do not explain the fall from the first quarter to the second, and a quarterly profit figure is not the best guide to a life insurer's performance, because accounting profit depends on timing of expenses and on valuation of policy liabilities. Univest says the supplied data did not explain what drove revenue or profit growth, and we do not speculate.

The figures that analysts follow most closely are value of new business (VNB) and its margin. VNB is the estimated present value of future profits from the policies sold in a period, and the VNB margin is that value divided by annualised premium equivalent (APE), a standard measure of new sales that counts regular premiums in full and single premiums at a tenth. For the half year, VNB was ₹2,037 crore, up 12.1%, and second-quarter VNB growth was 14.8%. The VNB margin was 24.7%, up from 24.5%. APE was ₹8,245 crore in total, up 11%, with individual APE of ₹7,080 crore, up 9%. Second-quarter APE overall was up 13%, and individual weighted received premium in the quarter was up 11%. Because VNB grew by about the same rate as APE, the margin was stable, which suggests the mix of products did not change much, though the reports do not give a product breakdown.

On premiums, new business premium was ₹19,126 crore, up 18%, renewal premium ₹20,443 crore, up 14%, and total premium ₹39,569 crore, up 16%. Renewal premium is the money from policies already on the books and is a sign of how well customers keep their policies. Total premium growing faster than APE reflects a business where single-premium and renewal income are both rising, but we cannot break this down with the data available. Assets under management were ₹4,09,673 crore, about ₹4.1 lakh crore, up 13.8%. Embedded value, a measure of the value of the in-force business plus net assets, was ₹66,461 crore, and the rolling 12-month operating return on embedded value was 14.9%.

On market position, HDFC Life's share of the individual-business market was 16.2%, up from 16.1% in the first quarter of FY27. Kotak Neo reports that the shares closed at ₹550.55 on the National Stock Exchange on October 15, up 1.19%, but this is a snapshot taken before the results were fully digested, and the sources do not report the reaction on later days. The Univest article also notes a return on equity of 11.54% for FY26 compared with 12.10% for FY25, which indicates that the company's accounting return on shareholder capital was a little lower than in the previous year; it does not give a figure for the current year.

How should a reader interpret the numbers? Growth of 11% to 12% in APE and VNB is solid, and the stable margin means that growth was not bought by cutting profitability. Profit growth of about 13% is in line. The quarter-on-quarter dip should not be over-read, since seasonality and the timing of items can move the quarterly profit. Compared with the earlier period the pace has moderated; the sources do not give previous-year growth rates to compare, so we say only that the figures show steady expansion. The company's size, with assets of about ₹4.1 lakh crore and a share of 16.2% of the individual market, means that its results are a useful read-across for the sector, although other insurers may show different trends.

What does it mean for customers? The results do not change any policy. For policyholders, the more relevant indicators are the solvency ratio and persistency, which the reports do not give, so readers who want those should look at HDFC Life's disclosures on its website and on the stock exchanges. For prospective buyers, a high VNB margin means the insurer earns a good return on new sales, which says nothing about whether a particular product is good value for the buyer; the usual advice is to compare cover, charges, claim settlement record and the product's suitability for your goals. This article is a news summary and not investment or insurance advice.
source_name: Kotak Neo and Univest (reporting HDFC Life's Q2 and H1 FY27 results, October 15-16, 2026)
image_alt: Office buildings representing an Indian life insurer (illustrative)
key_points: HDFC Life reported second-quarter FY27 profit after tax of ₹508 crore, up 13.3% from ₹448.29 crore a year earlier but down 16.9% from ₹611.19 crore in the first quarter; revenue was ₹21,727 crore, up 15.1%.
For the half year, profit was ₹1,119 crore, up 12.7%, and value of new business (VNB) was ₹2,037 crore, up 12.1%, with the VNB margin at 24.7% against 24.5%.
Annualised premium equivalent (APE) was ₹8,245 crore, up 11%; new business premium was ₹19,126 crore, up 18%, and total premium ₹39,569 crore, up 16%.
Assets under management were ₹4,09,673 crore, up 13.8%; embedded value was ₹66,461 crore and the rolling 12-month operating return on embedded value was 14.9%.
Individual market share was 16.2%, up from 16.1% in the first quarter; the shares closed at ₹550.55 on October 15, up 1.19%.
why_it_matters: HDFC Life is one of India's largest private life insurers, so its results show how the market for protection and savings policies is growing and how profitable new sales are. Value of new business and margin are the figures that matter most for life insurers, more than headline profit.

title: Aviva Launches a US Specialty Insurer Starting With Commercial Property in Q4 and Sets a Target of More Than £500 Million of Wealth Profit by 2032
summary: Aviva announced on October 7 a New York-based US specialty platform backed by its A+ rated UK insurer, and on October 16 told investors its Wealth arm is on track for £280 million of operating profit by 2027 and expects to exceed £500 million by 2032.
description:
Aviva, a large UK insurer, has made two announcements in two weeks that show where it expects growth. On October 7, 2026 it launched Aviva Specialty, a US specialty insurance platform based in New York. On October 16 it held a Wealth 'In Focus' briefing for investors and analysts, the first of its kind since 2023, at which it set out a profit target for the Wealth business. Both items come from Aviva's own announcements, namely its press release on the US launch and the regulatory announcement of the briefing. We have not reviewed the presentation slides or any recording of the briefing, so we report only the figures that the announcements contain.

Start with the US launch. Aviva Specialty is a wholly owned platform headquartered in New York City. It will start underwriting commercial property risks in the fourth quarter of 2026 and will serve the open-market brokerage channel and work with program administrators, in what Aviva calls a partnership-led model. Commercial property is the first line. The roadmap, according to the release, includes cyber, specialty and financial lines, and specialty casualty, with further expansion into delegated authority and program business. Policies will be written on the paper of Aviva Insurance Limited, which means that the UK insurer's balance sheet stands behind them; the release notes that Aviva Insurance Limited is rated A+ by AM Best as of September 2026, and it uses the name 'Aviva Insurance Ltd.' in one place, a minor inconsistency. The US legal entity is Aviva Specialty Insurance Services US, Inc., which does business as Aviva Specialty Insurance Agency Inc. in California and Florida.

Who is running it? Mike Karmilowicz is President of Aviva Specialty. He said what differentiates the business is 'the combination of a seasoned specialty insurance team' with a purpose-built platform. Jason Storah, chief executive of UK and Ireland General Insurance, called the launch an important step in Aviva's growth strategy and said the US offers significant growth opportunities, adding 'We are entering the market with a long-term perspective.' The release does not say how much capital Aviva is committing, how large it wants the US business to be, or when it expects it to be profitable, and it does not discuss the relationship with Direct Line, which Aviva owns, so we do not speculate on any of these. The release describes this as the first stage of a US specialty strategy and says Aviva will expand deliberately.

Why would a UK insurer go to the US? The release says only that the US offers significant opportunities. In general terms, the United States is the largest specialty insurance market in the world, and entering through brokers and program administrators lets a new insurer access business without building a large distribution network. The countervailing point, which the sources do not discuss, is that specialty markets are in a softer pricing cycle, so a new entrant must earn a place against established competitors. We note that other broker and insurer commentary in recent months has reported falling specialty rates, but we have not examined it for this article.

Now the Wealth briefing. Aviva's announcement says it is on track for £280 million of Wealth operating profit by 2027 and expects to exceed £500 million by 2032. Wealth operating profit has doubled since 2019, driven mainly by the Workplace and Adviser Platform propositions, which are the workplace pension business and the platforms used by financial advisers. Aviva says it is the UK's largest Wealth provider by assets, at £261 billion, with nearly six million Wealth customers, out of a UK customer base of 21.8 million. The briefing was hosted by group chief executive Amanda Blanc and presented by Doug Brown, chief executive of Insurance, Wealth and Retirement, and Michele Golunska, managing director of Wealth. Aviva describes the wealth market as 'a major growth opportunity and central to Aviva's long-term strategy'.

What drives the forecast? Aviva expects the UK wealth market to grow by more than 10% a year and, by 2035, an asset pool of £7.5 trillion and a profit pool of about £10 billion. These are Aviva's own projections and not independent estimates. It sees further organic growth potential in Direct Wealth, Advice and Targeted Support, a new regulatory approach that allows firms to give guidance to groups of customers. New technology, including artificial intelligence, and regulation such as the Pension Schemes Act 2026 and Targeted Support are cited as sources of opportunity. The announcement does not disclose net flow figures, so we cannot say how much new money Wealth is attracting.

The group figures come from both notes to editors. Aviva has 25.3 million customers and more than 325 years in business, paid £31.9 billion in claims and benefits in 2025, and had £479 billion of group assets under management and an estimated Solvency II shareholder capital surplus of £6.8 billion at June 30, 2026. The surplus is the amount of capital above the regulatory requirement.

What should readers make of this? The two announcements are a statement of strategy, not a set of results, and their numbers are targets that may or may not be met. For brokers in the US, there is a new potential source of commercial property capacity from Q4. For UK savers, the wealth push suggests Aviva will compete harder for workplace pensions and adviser platforms. For investors, the key tests are whether the US entry can be profitable in a soft market and whether Wealth reaches its profit targets. This article is a summary of company announcements and is not investment or insurance advice.

key_points: Aviva Specialty, a wholly owned US specialty platform based in New York, will start underwriting commercial property in the fourth quarter of 2026, working with open-market brokers and program administrators.
The roadmap includes cyber, specialty and financial lines, and specialty casualty; policies will be written on Aviva Insurance Limited paper, which AM Best rates A+ as of September 2026.
The release gives no capital commitment, premium target or financial target for the US business.
On October 16 Aviva said its Wealth operating profit is on track for £280 million by 2027, has doubled since 2019, and is expected to exceed £500 million by 2032.

Aviva calls itself the UK's largest wealth provider by assets (£261 billion), with nearly six million Wealth customers; group assets under management were £479 billion and the Solvency II surplus about £6.8 billion at June 30, 2026.
why_it_matters: A large UK insurer opening a US specialty arm and setting a long-term wealth profit target shows where it sees growth: in specialty risks that need underwriting expertise and in retirement and investment products. For brokers and savers it signals more competition in US commercial property and a bigger push into UK wealth.

title: OSFI's September Regulatory Release Sets November 1 Start for New Capital Rules, Opens a TLAC Consultation to November 9 and Updates Insurer Reporting for IFRS 18
summary: Canada's banking and insurance supervisor said its final Capital Adequacy Requirements guideline takes effect November 1, 2026, its mortgage insurer capital test (MICAT 2027) on January 1, 2027, and that insurance regulatory returns are being updated for IFRS 18, with the first final returns due January 1, 2027.
description:
Canada's federal financial regulator has set the dates by which banks and insurers must apply a series of new rules, and several of them arrive within weeks. The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) published its third quarterly regulatory release of 2026 on September 10, 2026. This article is based on the law firm Fasken's summary of that release. We have not reviewed OSFI's own documents, so the items below are as summarised, and anyone affected should read the guidelines themselves. The release covers capital, digital assets, interest rate risk and insurance reporting.

Start with capital. OSFI's final Capital Adequacy Requirements (CAR) Guideline for 2027 takes effect on November 1, 2026. It responds to a consultation held in November 2025. According to Fasken, the guideline is intended to improve clarity and consistency, to align capital requirements with risk and to reduce regulatory burden where possible. The CAR Guideline sets out how much capital banks must hold against the risks on their books, so a revision affects lending decisions across the system. The summary does not describe the specific changes, and we do not guess at them.

The second capital item is a consultation on the Total Loss Absorbing Capacity (TLAC) Guideline. TLAC rules require the largest banks to hold enough bail-in debt and capital so that a failing bank can be recapitalised without public money. OSFI proposes updates to clarify what it expects about the content and frequency of external legal opinions. The consultation lasts 60 days and closes on November 9, 2026. The third item is the capital test for mortgage insurers. The Mortgage Insurer Capital Adequacy Test for 2027 (MICAT 2027) takes effect on January 1, 2027. It recognises the lower risk of certain low-rise multi-unit residential construction projects, which should affect the capital that mortgage insurers must hold against such loans. The summary does not give the size of the change.

Digital assets are the next topic. The Crypto-asset Exposures (Banking) Guideline for 2027 takes effect on November 1, 2026 for institutions with an October 31 fiscal year-end and on January 1, 2027 for those with a December 31 year-end. According to Fasken, changes include recognising certain hedging arrangements across regulated exchanges when calculating capital for Group 2a crypto-assets, and excluding derivative exposures from client-clearing activities from the Group 2 exposure limit. OSFI also clarified its approach to tokenised and digitally represented deposits: it is technology-neutral and focuses on what a product or service is, not how it is built. Institutions using new technologies must still comply with all applicable laws, regulations and guidance. This is a signal that a bank cannot escape deposit rules by building a deposit product on a new technology.

Interest rate risk is covered in an update to Guideline B-12, which sets out how institutions manage interest rate risk. OSFI has updated the interest rate shock scenarios and clarified how to measure the effect of rate changes on earnings. The effective dates match the crypto-asset guideline: November 1, 2026 or January 1, 2027, depending on fiscal year-end. OSFI plans to finalise the draft amendment to its Pillar 3 disclosure on interest rate risk on November 19, 2026.

For insurers, the most direct item concerns financial reporting. OSFI has updated its insurance regulatory return templates to reflect the presentation and disclosure requirements of IFRS 18, the new accounting standard on presentation in financial statements. Fasken notes that the measurement of assets and liabilities is unchanged, so the change is about how numbers are laid out and not about their value. Insurers with December 31 year-ends face final returns on January 1, 2027, and those with October 31 year-ends face them on November 1, 2027. These returns are what the regulator uses to monitor insurers, so a change in templates requires insurers to adjust their systems and reporting processes.

OSFI held a virtual Industry Day on these updates on September 24, 2026. The key dates, as summarised, are as follows. November 1, 2026: the CAR Guideline takes effect, and the crypto-asset and B-12 changes apply to October 31 year-end institutions. November 9, 2026: the TLAC consultation closes. November 19, 2026: planned finalisation of the Pillar 3 interest rate risk disclosure amendment. January 1, 2027: MICAT 2027 takes effect, the crypto-asset and B-12 changes apply to December 31 year-end institutions, and the new insurance return templates apply to December 31 year-end insurers.

What does it mean for ordinary Canadians? Most people will not notice any change. Capital rules affect the cost and availability of credit gradually, and nothing in the summary says that mortgage rates or insurance premiums will change as a result. The MICAT change is relevant to the market for insured mortgages on low-rise multi-unit housing, but the summary does not quantify any effect. For the industry, the main work is compliance: updating capital calculations by November 1, preparing responses to the TLAC consultation by November 9 and rebuilding reporting for IFRS 18. Readers who work in a regulated institution should consult OSFI's website for the final documents. This article is a summary of a regulatory update and is not legal or compliance advice.
source_name: Fasken (summary of OSFI's third quarterly release of 2026, September 10, 2026)
image_alt: Financial documents and charts representing regulatory capital rules (illustrative)
key_points: OSFI's final Capital Adequacy Requirements (CAR) Guideline for 2027 takes effect on November 1, 2026, responding to a November 2025 consultation and aiming for clarity, risk alignment and less burden where possible.
A consultation on updates to the Total Loss Absorbing Capacity (TLAC) Guideline, about external legal opinions, runs for 60 days and closes on November 9, 2026.
MICAT 2027, the capital test for mortgage insurers, takes effect January 1, 2027 and recognises the lower risk of certain low-rise multi-unit residential construction projects.

Insurance regulatory return templates are updated for IFRS 18: insurers with December 31 year-ends face final returns on January 1, 2027, and those with October 31 year-ends on November 1, 2027; measurement of assets and liabilities is unchanged.

OSFI says its approach to tokenised and digitally represented deposits is technology-neutral, and a revised Guideline B-12 on interest rate risk has the same effective dates as the crypto-asset guideline (November 1, 2026 or January 1, 2027).
why_it_matters: Capital rules decide how much money Canadian banks and insurers must hold against losses, which affects what they can lend and how safe they are. Mortgage insurers and anyone who reads insurers' financial statements will see the effect of the January 2027 changes.
